content: In vector calculus, the gradient of a scalar field is a vector field that indicates the direction of the steepest increase of the scalar field. The magnitude of the gradient represents the maximum rate of change of the scalar field at a given point. For functions defined on a Banach space with vectorial values, the Jacobian generalizes the concept of the gradient. Interpretations of the Gradient Imagine a room where the temperature at each point ((x, y, z)) is described by a scalar field (T(x, y, z)), and the temperature does not vary with time. At any point in the room, the gradient of (T) points in the direction where the temperature increases most rapidly. The magnitude of the gradient quantifies how quickly the temperature rises in that direction. Consider a hill where the height above sea level at a point ((x, y)) is given by (H(x, y)). The gradient of (H) at any point is a vector pointing in the direction of the steepest slope at that point. The magnitude of the gradient vector represents the steepness of the slope. The gradient can also measure how the scalar field changes in other directions by taking the dot product with a unit vector in the desired direction. For example, if the steepest slope on a hill is 40%, a road going directly uphill will also have a maximum slope of 40%. However, if the road ascends at an angle to the uphill direction, its slope will be less steep. For instance, if the angle between the road and the uphill direction (projected onto the horizontal plane) is (60^circ), the slope along the road will be (20%), which is (40% times cos(60^circ)). Mathematically, if (H) is differentiable, the dot product of the gradient of (H) with a unit vector gives the slope of the hill in the direction of that vector. This is equivalent to the directional derivative of (H) in that direction. Formal Definition The gradient (or gradient vector field) of a scalar function (f(x)) with respect to a vector variable (x = (x_1, dots, x_n)) is denoted by (nabla f) or (vec{nabla} f), where (nabla) (the nabla symbol) represents the vector differential operator, also known as del. The notation (operatorname{grad}(f)) is also used for the gradient. By definition, the gradient is a vector field whose components are the partial derivatives of (f). That is: [ nabla f = left( frac{partial f}{partial x_1}, frac{partial f}{partial x_2}, dots, frac{partial f}{partial x_n} right) ] The dot product of the gradient at a point (x) with a vector (v) gives the directional derivative of (f) at (x) in the direction of (v). Consequently, the gradient of (f) is orthogonal to the level sets of (f). This property also demonstrates that the gradient, although defined in terms of coordinates, is invariant under orthogonal transformations, consistent with its geometric interpretation. Because the gradient is orthogonal to level sets, it can be used to construct a vector normal to a surface (e.g., a surface in 3D or a curve in 2D). The gradient is an irrotational vector field, meaning that line integrals through a gradient field are path-independent and can be evaluated using the gradient theorem. Conversely, an irrotational vector field in a simply connected region is always the gradient of some function. Expressions for the Gradient in 3 Dimensions The form of the gradient depends on the coordinate system used: In Cartesian coordinates: [ nabla f = left( frac{partial f}{partial x}, frac{partial f}{partial y}, frac{partial f}{partial z} right) ] In cylindrical coordinates: [ nabla f = left( frac{partial f}{partial rho}, frac{1}{rho} frac{partial f}{partial theta}, frac{partial f}{partial z} right) ] where (theta) is the azimuthal angle and (z) is the axial coordinate. In spherical coordinates: [ nabla f = left( frac{partial f}{partial r}, frac{1}{r} frac{partial f}{partial theta}, frac{1}{r sin theta} frac{partial f}{partial phi} right) ] where (phi) is the azimuthal angle and (theta) is the zenith angle. The Gradient and the Derivative or Differential The gradient of a function (f) from Euclidean space (mathbb{R}^n) to (mathbb{R}) at a point (x_0 in mathbb{R}^n) characterizes the best linear approximation to (f) at (x_0). For (x) close to (x_0), the approximation is given by: [ f(x) approx f(x_0) + (nabla f)_{x_0} cdot (x x_0) ] Here, ((nabla f)_{x_0}) is the gradient of (f) computed at (x_0), and the dot denotes the dot product in (mathbb{R}^n). This equation corresponds to the first two terms in the multivariable Taylor series expansion of (f) at (x_0). The differential (or total derivative) of (f) at a point (x) in (mathbb{R}^n) is a linear map from (mathbb{R}^n) to (mathbb{R}), often denoted by (mathrm{d}f_x) or (Df(x)). The gradient is related to the differential by the formula: [ mathrm{d}f_x(v) = nabla f cdot v ] for any (v in mathbb{R}^n). The function (mathrm{d}f), which maps (x) to (mathrm{d}f_x), is called the differential or exterior derivative of (f) and is an example of a differential 1-form. Covariance of the Gradient The differential is more natural than the gradient because it is invariant under all coordinate transformations (or diffeomorphisms), whereas the gradient is only invariant under orthogonal transformations due to the implicit use of the dot product in its definition. For this reason, the distinction between the two concepts is often blurred using the notions of covariant and contravariant vectors. From this perspective, the components of the gradient transform covariantly under changes of coordinates, so it is called a covariant vector field, whereas the components of a vector field in the usual sense transform contravariantly. The Gradient on Riemannian Manifolds For any smooth function (f) on a Riemannian manifold ((M, g)), the gradient of (f) is the vector field (nabla f) such that for any vector field (X): [ g_x(nabla f, X) = partial_X f ] Here, (g_x(cdot, cdot)) denotes the inner product of tangent vectors at (x) defined by the metric (g), and (partial_X f) (sometimes denoted (X(f))) is the function that maps any point (x in M) to the directional derivative of (f) in the direction (X), evaluated at (x). In local coordinates, the gradient can be expressed in terms of the metric and the exterior derivative (df). The gradient (nabla f) is the vector field associated with the differential 1-form (df) using the musical isomorphism (sharp) defined by the metric (g). This relationship generalizes the case of (mathbb{R}^n), where the metric is the flat metric given by the dot product.
